paragraphs: The third charge against the House of Representatives is that its members will come from the class of citizens with the least sympathy for the mass of the people. That class, the charge says, is the one most likely to aim at ambitiously sacrificing the many to the aggrandizement of the few.

Of all the objections raised against the federal Constitution, this may be the most extraordinary. It is aimed at a supposed oligarchy, yet its principle attacks the very root of republican government.

Every political constitution has, or ought to have, two aims. The first is to obtain as rulers the men with the most wisdom to see, and the most virtue to pursue, the common good of society. The second is to take the most effective precautions to keep them virtuous for as long as they hold public trust. Choosing rulers by election is the characteristic policy of republican government. This form of government relies on many different means to prevent its rulers from degenerating, and the most effective is to limit the term of office so that rulers stay properly accountable to the people.

Let me now ask what feature of the House of Representatives violates the principles of republican government or helps the few rise on the ruins of the many. Is not every feature, on the contrary, strictly in line with those principles? Is not each one scrupulously fair to the rights and claims of every class and description of citizens?

Who will elect the federal representatives? Not the rich rather than the poor, not the learned rather than the ignorant, not the haughty heirs of distinguished names rather than the humble sons of obscurity and bad fortune. The electors will be the great body of the people of the United States. They will be the same people who, in every State, have the right to elect the corresponding branch of the State legislature.

Who may the people choose? Any citizen whose merit earns him the esteem and confidence of his country. No requirement of wealth, birth, religious faith or occupation is allowed to bind the people's judgment or thwart their inclination.

Consider the position of the men on whom the free votes of their fellow citizens may confer the representative trust. We shall find that it carries every security anyone could devise or desire for their faithfulness to their constituents.

In the first place, the preference of their fellow citizens will have set them apart. We may presume, then, that in general they will also be somewhat distinguished by the qualities that earn such a preference, and that promise a sincere and scrupulous respect for the commitments they take on.

In the second place, they will enter public service in circumstances that must produce, at least for a time, some affection for their constituents. Every heart is sensitive to marks of honor, favor, esteem and confidence, and apart from any thought of interest, that sensitivity is some pledge of grateful and kindly returns. People often speak bitterly of ingratitude as a failing of human nature, and I must admit that examples of it, in public and private life alike, are all too frequent and glaring. But the universal and extreme indignation it arouses is itself proof of how strong and widespread the opposite feeling is.

In the third place, motives of a more selfish kind strengthen the ties that bind a representative to his constituents. His pride and vanity attach him to a form of government that supports his claims and gives him a share in its honors and distinctions. A few aspiring characters may harbor hopes or schemes of their own. Still, a great proportion of men who owe their advancement to their influence with the people will generally have more to hope for from keeping that favor than from changes in the government that would destroy the people's authority.

All these securities, however, would prove very insufficient without the restraint of frequent elections. So, in the fourth place, the House of Representatives is built to keep its members constantly mindful that they depend on the people. The feelings left on their minds by the way they were raised to office will not have time to fade under the exercise of power. They will be forced to look ahead to the moment when their power ends, when their use of it will be reviewed, and when they must come down to the level from which they rose. There they will stay forever, unless faithful performance of their trust has earned them a renewal of it.

I will add a fifth circumstance that restrains the House of Representatives from oppressive measures: they can make no law that will not apply with full force to themselves and their friends as well as to the great mass of society. This has always been counted among the strongest bonds human policy can forge between rulers and people. It creates a community of interests and a sympathy of feelings between them, of which few governments have given examples, and without which every government degenerates into tyranny. Someone may ask what will stop the House of Representatives from passing laws that discriminate in favor of themselves and a particular class of society. I answer: the character of the whole system; the nature of just and constitutional laws; and above all, the vigilant and manly spirit that moves the people of America, a spirit that nourishes liberty and is nourished by it in return.
If that spirit is ever so degraded that the people tolerate a law not binding on the legislature as well as on themselves, they will be ready to tolerate anything but liberty.

Such will be the relation between the House of Representatives and its constituents. Duty, gratitude, interest and even ambition are the cords that will bind members to fidelity and sympathy with the great mass of the people. It is possible that all of these together may fail to control the caprice and wickedness of man. But are they not everything that government will allow, and everything human prudence can devise? Are they not the genuine and characteristic means by which republican government provides for the liberty and happiness of the people? Are they not the very means on which every State government in the Union relies to achieve these important ends? What, then, are we to make of the objection this paper has fought? What are we to say to men who profess the most flaming zeal for republican government and yet boldly attack its fundamental principle? They claim to champion the right and capacity of the people to choose their own rulers, and yet they maintain that the people will prefer only those who will immediately and infallibly betray the trust given them.

Imagine someone who had not seen the method the Constitution prescribes for choosing representatives reading this objection. He could suppose nothing less than one of three things. Perhaps an unreasonable property qualification was attached to the right to vote. Perhaps the right to be elected was limited to people of particular families or fortunes. Or at the least, perhaps the method set by the State constitutions had been grossly departed from in some way. We have seen how badly such a supposition would err on the first two points. It would be no less mistaken on the last. The only difference we can find between the two cases is this: each representative of the United States will be elected by five or six thousand citizens, while in the individual States a representative is elected by about as many hundreds. Will anyone pretend that this difference justifies an attachment to the State governments and an abhorrence of the federal government? If the objection turns on this point, it deserves examination.

Does REASON support it? That cannot be said without maintaining that five or six thousand citizens are less able to choose a fit representative, or more easily corrupted by an unfit one, than five or six hundred. Reason tells us the opposite. In so large a number a fit representative is more likely to be found, and the choice is less likely to be drawn away from him by the intrigues of the ambitious or the ambitious or the bribes of the rich.

Can we accept the CONSEQUENCE of this doctrine? Suppose we say that five or six hundred citizens are as many as can jointly exercise the right to vote. Then must we not deprive the people of direct choice of their public servants wherever the administration of government does not need as many servants as one for each such number of citizens?

Do FACTS warrant the doctrine? The last paper showed that real representation in the British House of Commons very little exceeds the proportion of one for every thirty thousand inhabitants. There are also many powerful causes there, absent here, that favor the claims of rank and wealth. No one can be a representative of a county unless he owns real estate with a clear value of six hundred pounds sterling a year, or of a city or borough unless he owns a like estate of half that yearly value. Besides this requirement for county representatives, there is another for county electors: the vote is restricted to persons with a freehold estate worth more than twenty pounds sterling a year, at the present value of money. Despite these unfavorable circumstances, and despite some very unequal laws in the British code, no one can say that the representatives of that nation have raised the few on the ruins of the many.

But we do not need to look to foreign experience on this subject. Our own is explicit and decisive. The districts in New Hampshire where the people directly choose senators are nearly as large as her congressional districts will need to be. Those in Massachusetts are larger than needed for that purpose, and those in New York larger still. In New York, the members of Assembly for the cities and counties of New York and Albany are elected by very nearly as many voters as will be entitled to a representative in Congress, if we calculate on sixty-five representatives only. It makes no difference that in these senatorial districts and counties each elector votes for several representatives at once. If the same electors can choose four or five representatives at one time, they cannot be unable to choose one. Pennsylvania is another example. Some of her counties, which elect her State representatives, are almost as large as the districts that will elect her federal representatives. The city of Philadelphia is believed to hold between fifty and sixty thousand souls, so it will make up nearly two districts for choosing federal representatives. Yet it forms only one county, in which every elector votes for each of its representatives in the State legislature. And what may seem still more to our purpose, the whole city actually elects a SINGLE MEMBER of the executive council. The same is true of all the other counties of the State.

Are these facts not the most satisfactory proof of the fallacy used against this branch of the federal government? Has experience shown that the senators of New Hampshire, Massachusetts and New York, or the executive council of Pennsylvania, or the members of the Assembly in the last two States, have displayed any special disposition to sacrifice the many to the few? Has it shown them any less worthy of their places than the representatives and public officials chosen in other States by very small divisions of the people?

But some cases are stronger than any I have yet quoted. One branch of the legislature of Connecticut is set up so that each of its members is elected by the whole State. So is the governor of that State, of Massachusetts and of this State, and so is the president of New Hampshire. I leave every man to decide whether the outcome of any of these experiments can be said to support a suspicion that a broad mode of choosing the people's representatives tends to raise up traitors and undermine public liberty.
